b: Key concepts: Pathogenesis · Morphology · Clinical features · Prognosis · Transformation
Follicular lymphoma constitutes 40% of adult NHLs in the United States and is much less common in Asian populations.

Pathogenesis — neoplastic cells express BCL2 , which is absent from normal germinal centre B cells. 85% of tumours have a (14;18) translocation fusing the BCL2 gene (chromosome 18) to the IgH locus (chromosome 14) → inappropriate BCL2 overe

Morphology — lymph nodes show a distinctly nodular (follicular) proliferation. Neoplastic cells resemble germinal centre B cells — predominantly small "cleaved" cells (centrocytes) with angular nuclei and linear infoldings, mixed with varia

snip.t: Lymphocyte count isn't part of IPI (note: it IS part of the related FLIPI for follicular lymphoma).

The translocation is t(8;14) — c-myc is on chromosome 8, translocated to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus on chromosome 14 (not 18). bcl-2 is the chromosome 18 gene (relevant in follicular lymphoma's t(14;18), a different entity).
Splenomegaly: Lymphoid infiltration of the spleen; common in CLL, follicular lymphoma, and some aggressive subtypes.
Transformation: follicular lymphoma can transform into DLBCL.
Follicular lymphoma = t(14;18) = BCL2; mantle cell = t(11;14) = cyclin D1; Burkitt = t(8;14) = MYC, with the "starry sky" histology; ALCL = t(2;5) = ALK.
Follicular lymphomas may not be isolated to a single node.
Follicular lymphoma — t(14;18) → BCL-2 overexpression → resistance to apoptosis

qs.q: The anti-apoptotic effect of BCL-2 overexpression in follicular lymphoma occurs through which intracellular mechanism?
o: Stabilization of mitochondrial membrane and cytochrome c inhibition
qs.e: BCL-2 keeps the mitochondrial membrane intact, preventing cytochrome c release and blocking the intrinsic apoptotic pathway. Caspase activation and BAD upregulation are pro-apoptotic processes, not inhibited by BCL-2.

qs.q: A 55-year-old man presents with painless lymphadenopathy, and a lymph node biopsy reveals follicular lymphoma with t(14;18) translocation. Overexpression of the BCL-2 protein in this tumor promotes cell survival through which process?
qs.e: BCL-2 keeps the mitochondrial outer membrane intact, preventing cytochrome c release and blocking the intrinsic apoptotic pathway. Caspase inactivation is a different downstream process.
qs.s: Pathology by Dr. Irungu — — Oncopathology: MCQs

qs.q: Which genetic alteration is the hallmark of Follicular Lymphoma and results in the inhibition of apoptosis via BCL-2 overexpression?
qs.e: The t(14;18) translocation causes BCL-2 overexpression, which inhibits apoptosis in follicular lymphoma. The t(11;14) translocation instead leads to Cyclin D1 overexpression in mantle cell lymphoma.

qs.q: A patient with follicular lymphoma harbours the t(14;18) chromosomal translocation, resulting in the overexpression of BCL-2. How does this molecular alteration primarily promote tumour survival?
o: Upregulating Fas receptors on the cell surface to evade immune surveillance
Preventing cytochrome c release from mitochondria to block intrinsic apoptosis
Hypermethylating CpG islands within tumour suppressor promoters to silence genes
Stabilising HIF-1 alpha under normoxia to induce uncoordinated sprouting
qs.e: BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that prevents cytochrome c release through mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation, blocking intrinsic apoptosis. Upregulation of Fas receptors is not caused by BCL-2, which instead inhibits cell death directly at the mitochondrial level.
qs.s: Molecular Basis of Cancer: Cell Cycle, Apoptosis & Angiogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: Follicular lymphoma frequently involves the overexpression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2. Which genetic aberration is responsible for this alteration?
qs.e: Follicular lymphoma is characterized by the t(14;18) translocation, leading to BCL2 overexpression and evasion of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway. Translocation t(9;22) is found in CML.
qs.s: Hallmarks of Cancer: Molecular Basis, Cell Cycle & Oncogenes: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with follicular lymphoma treated with chemoimmunotherapy develops progressive cognitive decline and visual changes. MRI of the brain shows asymmetric white matter lesions without mass effect. Which underlying therapy contributed to this opportunistic infection?
o: Rituximab therapy targeting CD20 B cells
qs.e: Depletion of B cells via anti-CD20 therapy impairs humoral immunity and predisposes patients to JC virus reactivation leading to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Targeted kinase inhibitors or proteasome inhibitors do not share this specific association with JC virus reactivation.

qs.q: The anti-apoptotic effect of BCL-2 overexpression, as seen in follicular lymphoma, occurs due to which mechanism?
o: Activation of the p53 tumor suppressor
qs.e: BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that resides in the mitochondrial membrane. Its overexpression stabilizes the mitochondrial membrane, preventing the release of pro-apoptotic factors like cytochrome c into the cytoplasm, thereby blocking the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 16, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: The anti-apoptotic effect of BCL-2 overexpression in follicular lymphoma occurs due to:
o: Stimulation of the extrinsic apoptotic pathway
Inhibition of pro‑apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BAK
qs.e: BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein. Overexpression of BCL-2, as seen in follicular lymphoma (often due to the t(14;18) translocation), prevents the activation of pro-apoptotic proteins (like BAX and BAK) and thus inhibits the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis, leading to increased cell survival.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - October 9, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

es.q: Identify the characteristic chromosomal translocation and the associated oncogene overexpression found in Follicular Lymphoma and Mantle Cell Lymphoma.
es.m: Follicular Lymphoma is characterized by the t(14;18) translocation, leading to BCL-2 overexpression. Mantle Cell Lymphoma is characterized by the t(11;14) translocation, leading to Cyclin D1 overexpression.
es.s: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: Classification, Symptoms, Diagnosis, and Treatment — Pract

es.q: Identify the characteristic chromosomal translocation and associated oncogene overexpression for TWO of the following Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma subtypes: Follicular Lymphoma, Mantle Cell Lymphoma, Burkitt Lymphoma, Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL).
es.m: 1. **Follicular Lymphoma:** Characteristic translocation is t(14;18), leading to BCL-2 overexpression. 2. **Mantle Cell Lymphoma:** Characteristic translocation is t(11;14), leading to Cyclin D1 overexpression. 3. **Burkitt Lymphoma:** Characteristic translocation is t(8;14), leading to MYC overexpression. 4. **Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL):** Characteristic translocation is t(2;5), leading to ALK overexpression. *(Candidates need to provide two correct pairs for full marks)*
es.s: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: Classification, Symptoms, Diagnosis, and Treatment — Pract

es.q: For Follicular Lymphoma and Mantle Cell Lymphoma, identify the characteristic chromosomal translocation and the specific oncogene overexpressed due to this translocation, as detailed in the article.
es.m: 1. **Follicular Lymphoma:** * **Translocation:** t(14;18) * **Oncogene Overexpression:** BCL-2 2. **Mantle Cell Lymphoma:** * **Translocation:** t(11;14) * **Oncogene Overexpression:** Cyclin D1
es.s: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: Classification, Symptoms, Diagnosis, and Treatment — Pract

es.q: A pathology report for a patient with NHL mentions specific chromosomal translocations. State the characteristic chromosomal translocation and the associated overexpressed oncogene for *two* of the following NHL subtypes: Follicular lymphoma, Mantle cell lymphoma, or Burkitt lymphoma.
es.m: The characteristic chromosomal translocations and associated oncogenes for specific NHL subtypes are: 1. **Follicular lymphoma**: t(14;18); BCL-2 overexpression. 2. **Mantle cell lymphoma**: t(11;14); Cyclin D1 overexpression. 3. **Burkitt lymphoma**: t(8;14); MYC overexpression. *(Students must provide any two of these.)*

ai.title: Follicular Lymphoma
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Follicular lymphoma is an indolent B‑cell non‑Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by nodular growth and BCL2 over‑expression due to t(14;18). It presents with painless lymphadenopathy and may transform to aggressive disease.

sections.p: Follicular lymphoma (FL) is a germinal‑centre B‑cell neoplasm with a nodular architecture. Diagnosis requires histology showing a mixture of centrocytes and centroblasts and confirmation of the t(14;18) translocation or BCL2 over‑expression.
b: Nodular pattern on excisional lymph node biopsy
Centrocytes (small cleaved cells) dominate; ≤5 centroblasts/HPF = grade 1, 6‑15 = grade 2, >15 = grade 3
Immunophenotype: CD20+, CD10+, BCL2+, BCL6+, Ki‑67 low

t.b: Confirms histologic grade and architecture; essential for definitive diagnosis

t.a: FISH for t(14;18) or PCR for IGH‑BCL2
t.b: Detects the hallmark translocation; if unavailable, rely on immunohistochemistry for BCL2

t.a: Flow cytometry of fine‑needle aspirate (if biopsy not feasible)
t.b: Shows clonal CD19+/CD20+ B‑cells with light‑chain restriction; supports diagnosis when tissue not accessible

sections.p: Staging follows the Ann Ann Arbor system (I–IV) and the FL International Prognostic Index (FLIPI) predicts outcome.
b: Ann Ann Arbor stage based on nodal/extranodal sites and systemic symptoms
FLIPI factors: age > 60, hemoglobin < 12 g/dL, LDH ↑, >4 nodal sites, stage III/IV

t.a: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (or ultrasound where CT unavailable)
t.b: Assigns Ann Ann Arbor stage; if imaging not possible, clinical exam and chest X‑ray give approximate stage

t.a: Baseline labs (CBC, LDH, β2‑microglobulin, hepatitis B/C serology)
t.b: Provides FLIPI variables; guides risk‑adapted therapy

sections.p: FL arises from acquired genetic events; the dominant cause is the t(14;18)(q32;q21) translocation leading to BCL2 over‑expression. In low‑resource settings, co‑existing infections (HIV, hepatitis B) can accelerate disease or affect treatment choices.
b: t(14;18) translocation → BCL2 over‑expression (apoptosis resistance)
Chronic immune stimulation (e.g., HIV infection)
Environmental factors: pesticide exposure, chronic antigenic drive

t.b: Identifies co‑infection that may alter prognosis and dictate antiretroviral therapy before chemotherapy

sections.p: Patients usually have painless, generalized lymphadenopathy. B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) are less common early but may appear with higher grade or transformation.
b: Enlarged, non‑tender peripheral nodes
Occasional splenomegaly
Rarely, extranodal masses (e.g., gastrointestinal polyps)

sections.p: A stepwise approach balances diagnostic certainty with resource constraints.
b: Physical exam for nodal distribution and organomegaly
Basic labs: CBC, LDH, liver/renal function

t.b: Detects splenomegaly or intra‑abdominal nodes when CT unavailable
Assesses marrow involvement; required for staging if peripheral blood shows cytopenias
Defines metabolic activity, helps detect transformation; if not available, rely on CT and clinical assessment

sections.p: Rapid nodal growth, new B symptoms, or laboratory evidence of transformation demand urgent reassessment.
b: Transformation to diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL)
Hyperviscosity from high tumor burden
Severe cytopenias from marrow infiltration

sections.p: Therapy is risk‑adapted. Low‑grade, asymptomatic disease may be observed; symptomatic or high‑risk disease requires immunochemotherapy.
b: Watch‑and‑wait for stage I–II, grade 1–2, no B symptoms
R‑CHOP (rituximab + cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) for symptomatic or high‑grade disease
R‑CVP (rituximab + cyclophosphamide, vincristine, prednisone) when anthracycline toxicity is a concern

t.b: Targets CD20 on B‑cells; essential for all chemo‑regimens; avoid in active hepatitis B without prophylaxis
Alkylating agent; preferred over doxorubicin if cardiac disease or limited monitoring of cardiac function

t.a: Supportive care – growth factor (G‑CSF) if neutropenia risk high, prophylactic antibiotics in HIV
t.b: Reduces infection risk; G‑CSF use guided by ANC < 500 µL

sections.p: Long‑term surveillance detects relapse or transformation.
b: Clinical review every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then 6–12 months
CBC, LDH, and physical exam at each visit
Repeat imaging (ultrasound or CT) if new symptoms or rising LDH

sections.p: Several indolent lymphomas share nodular patterns.
b: Mantle‑cell lymphoma – cyclin D1 positivity, t(11;14)
Nodular lymphocyte‑predominant Hodgkin lymphoma – CD20+, CD15‑, CD30‑
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia – diffuse pattern, CD5+

sections.p: Certain findings may appear normal despite active disease.
b: LDH can be normal in low‑grade FL; do not rely on it alone for staging
Peripheral blood may lack circulating lymphoma cells; marrow biopsy still required if suspicion high

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in node size, new B symptoms, or rapid rise in LDH – possible transformation
Severe cytopenias causing infection or bleeding

faq.q: Why is rituximab used in all regimens?
faq.a: It binds CD20, depleting malignant B‑cells and improves response rates without adding significant organ toxicity.
It is generally incurable but highly controllable; long‑term remission is common with appropriate therapy.
In asymptomatic, low‑grade disease without bulky nodes or organ compromise, observation avoids unnecessary toxicity.

exam: A 45‑year‑old with painless cervical nodes and no B symptoms – what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Excisional node biopsy to obtain histology and grade; fine‑needle aspirate is insufficient.
How does the t(14;18) translocation drive follicular lymphoma pathogenesis? — It places BCL2 under the IGH enhancer, causing over‑expression of an anti‑apoptotic protein.
A patient on R‑CHOP develops rising transaminases – which drug is most likely responsible and what should you do? — Doxorubicin is hepatotoxic; consider dose reduction or switch to R‑CVP.

What features on histology distinguish grade 3 follicular lymphoma from transformed DLBCL? — Grade 3 has >15 centroblasts/HPF but retains follicular architecture; DLBCL shows diffuse sheets of large cells.

In a low‑resource clinic without PET‑CT, how would you assess for transformation? — Rely on rapid clinical deterioration, new B symptoms, rising LDH, and repeat CT or ultrasound plus repeat biopsy of the most suspicious node.

Why is anthracycline (doxorubicin) avoided in patients with limited cardiac monitoring? — It can cause irreversible cardiomyopathy; without echocardiography you should use anthracycline‑free regimens.

How does HIV infection modify the management of follicular lymphoma? — Requires antiretroviral therapy, prophylaxis for hepatitis B reactivation, and may favor less intensive chemo due to immunosuppression.
What red‑flag laboratory change suggests transformation to aggressive lymphoma? — Sudden LDH rise > 2 × upper limit of normal or new cytopenias.
